speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the entire house. On Friday morning, June 14, there was delivered to a Calgary law office at 9.30 a.m., by the first morning mail delivery, a memorandum entitled "Proposed Changes in Canadian Taxes". The memorandum summarizes the budget, has a budget resolutions index and attached to it are appendices containing the budget resolutions. The whole runs to 25 pages and is under a covering letter from Clarkson, Gordon and Company of Toronto. The envelope containing this material is metered, and the meter stamp bears the date of June 14.
The question which arises is how this material could have been prepared multi-graphed and delivered by ordinary mail to a Calgary office by 9.30 a.m. on Friday after evening. It may be possible that this analysis of the budget could have been prepared, the of the budget could have been prepared, the material mimeographed and the whole dispatched to Calgary, and I presume to every other city in Canada, and then delivered within the times I have given. However, it seems somewhat improbable.
I have checked the T.C.A. schedules to Calgary and find that only one plane leaves Toronto for Calgary after eight o'clock in the evening. This plane is a Vanguard which leaves Toronto at 2.50 a.m. and arrives in Calgary at 6.20 a.m. Calgary time. I have also checked with the post office as to what time a letter would need to be mailed in Toronto to catch this plane and whether it would be delivered on the first mail delivery in Calgary. I was informed that a letter would normally need to be mailed in Toronto by 10 p.m. to get out to the airport in time for this plane. If it were on the plane it might or might not be delivered in Calgary on the first delivery, depending on whether the plane arrived on time and on the volume of mail to be handled, matters which it has been impossible for me to check. In view of this the metered date of June 14 on the letter in question seems odd, particularly as the covering letter bears the date of June 13.
I believe the house is entitled to a full explanation of this matter in view of the questions which have been raised in regard to preserving the secrecy of the budget.
Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of
Finance): I am hardly in a position to speak on this matter without looking into it, mainly because I am no longer a member of Clarkson, Gordon and Company. I do know that for many, many years that firm, as well as many other firms in all parts of Canada, including all the banks and various other institutions, have received copies of the budget speech after it has been delivered in this house from the offices of the Bank of Canada in their area. I know that this particular firm, Clarkson, Gordon and Company, have in the past made a point of summarizing the main points in the budget that night and issuing them that night or the following morning at an early hour. Apart from that, I am not in a position to say anything about this matter until I make inquiries.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschatelets (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time ago the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) asked me for a statement in connection with the organization of the universal exhibition of 1967, and I want to make such a statement today, as I promised him last Friday.
On April 27, 1963, I was, as federal minister, entrusted with the responsibility of organizing the world exhibition of 1967.
Before April 27, 1963, the former administration had taken various steps in this respect.
(1)	The house passed, on December 20, 1962, a bill in view of setting up the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation. The legislation provided that the corporation would plan, organize and administer the exhibition which was to be held on Montreal island, for a period of six months during the year 1967. A commissioner and a deputy commissioner were appointed to that effect.
(2)	Apart from this legislation, a three way agreement was reached in order to choose a site for the exhibition, which basically imposed upon the city of Montreal the responsibility of supplying that site to the World Exhibition Corporation. The site was also to be approved by the federal government in agreement with the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec.
(3)	Under the three way agreement concluded on March 25, 1963, Mayor Drapeau recommended, on behalf of the city of Montreal, a site in the St. Lawrence river which would comprise the island of St. Helene, Round island, as well as an enlargement of those islands obtained by dumping All in the river. A third island would, moreover, be built along the seawall of the St. Lawrence seaway, and would be known as Notre Dame island. The total acreage thus created would be 600 acres. The mayor informed the former administration that the provincial government approved the site.

(4)	On March 28, 1963, the former prime minister of Canada advised the mayor of Montreal that the federal government would accept his proposal on condition that the legislation establishing the corporation which stipulated that the exhibition be held on Montreal island be amended, and, second, on condition that the proposed work be approved under the terms of the Navigable Waters Protection Act when detailed plans were available.
Unofficial discussions, which began on April 24, were then held between officials of the federal government and representatives of the city of Montreal and their consultants on a complete study of the proposal.
On April 25, the Department of Public Works received from the director of public works of the city of Montreal a request for a preliminary agreement regarding the filling up of the "A" area, which is that section of the site connecting Round island to St. Helen's island.
Following that request, a meeting took place in Montreal on May 1, which was attended by federal officials of the Department of Public Works, of the Department of Transport, of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, of the national harbours board and their consultants, in order to reconsider the proposition.
During the meeting, some technical questions were directed to the representatives of the city of Montreal about the possible effects of the planned construction on the chosen site. The city provided information on the program of studies of scale models and other technical studies being carried out. Together with federal officials, the city has established a plan of action in order to be able to supply as soon as possible the technical data and a detailed plan.
It was imperative to reach a prompt decision, even if only temporary, so that the international bureau of exhibitions might receive by May 14 a plan elaborate enough to enable it, if it saw fit, to choose Montreal as the site of the 1967 exhibition.
Meetings were held on May 9, in Ottawa, with Mayor Drapeau, who told the federal government that the city of Montreal would be able to prepare the site and to give it over to the corporation on June 30, 1964.
During those discussions with the mayor of Montreal it was clearly established that, should the proposed site be accepted, the city of Montreal would see to it that the work would not impede navigation on the river and would fully comply with the regulations set out in the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
After that meeting and other discussions, and in view of the fact that a report had to be submitted to the international bureau in

Paris on May 12, 1963, I advised Mayor Drapeau, on behalf of the federal government, on May 10, 1963, that we accepted the site on the conditions mentioned in the telegram sent by the former prime minister on March 28.
I attended the meeting of the international bureau in Paris with the commissioner general and other members of the corporation as well as Mayor Drapeau, at which time the project concerning the site of the exhibition was submitted.
On May 17, we agreed to grant the city of Montreal prior consent concerning the filling up of section "A", between St. Helen's island and Round island.
It is important to note that the prior consent granted in connection with section "A", bears on works that the city of Montreal had thought of carrying out before the world fair, and it was established that such works would not become a hazard to navigation or have any effect on the water level.
Federal officials and municipal representatives met to examine the results of model and other engineering studies undertaken by the city. The last meetings were held on June 11 and 12. It is yet too soon to tell the final results of those studies. The city of Montreal is at present considering the whole problem and we shall shortly receive, I hope, a detailed plan covering not only this site but also work connected with the site, such as source of backfilling materials, various items of required machinery and equipment etc., in order to ensure that the site will be ready by June 30, 1964 and that such works will not be a hazard to navigation on the St. Lawrence river or the seaway.
I intend to call a general meeting of all parties concerned with the 1967 world fair, such meeting to be held here in Ottawa in the first week of July; the parties concerned are the federal government's departmental committee, the provincial minister responsible for the fair, the mayor of Montreal, and the fair commissioners. At that time we shall have received additional information from the consulting engineers.
Once the preliminary work is completed, I intend to report to the house from time to time on the progress of the project, because this undertaking is national in its scope and concerns all Canadians.
I hope, if and when it is possible, to invite a group of members to Montreal to see the works and the master plan for the fair.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been impressed with the evidence which has been presented to me in numerous reports concerning the increasing lung cancer death

Health and Welfare
rate in Canada and the serious health problem that is posed by this disease. There is scientific evidence that cigarette smoking is a contributory cause of lung cancer, and that it may also be associated with chronic bronchitis and coronary heart disease.
Health agencies, including the Department of National Health and Welfare, have a duty to inform the public about the risk to health connected with cigarette smoking. It seems to me that special efforts should be made to dissuade children and young people from acquiring the habit.
In initiating a program directed to the reduction or elimination of this health hazard it will be essential, if the best possible results are to be achieved, for the Department of National Health and Welfare to work in close co-operation with provincial health and other departments, voluntary health agencies, professional associations and other groups concerned with this problem. It has therefore been decided to call an early conference to consider this matter, and I am writing to interested groups inviting them to meet with me in Ottawa. Invitations will go to the provinces through the provincial ministers of health. In addition, professional and voluntary health agencies interested in this matter will be invited to attend, as well as representatives of the tobacco industry and growers.
It is hoped that at this conference there will be a full discussion of the evidence linking cigarette smoking with lung cancer and other conditions, and that proposals can be made for a positive and effective program regarding this problem.

subtopic: TRAINING OF CUSTODIAL PERSONNEL IN PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Guards in Canadian
penitentiaries receive, on appointment, an average of two weeks induction training. During the first six months of service, a recruit is closely supervised by his immediate superiors and by the staff training officer. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this department is, of course, concerned to see that suitable motels and other public service facilities are available for visitors to the national parks of Canada, whether located on the route of the trans-Canada highway or not. It is the general policy that motels, hotels, cabin developments and restaurants be provided by private enterprise. These will in future increasingly be located in visitor service centres in order better to serve both park visitors and the general travelling public. As the need arises for such facilities the normal procedure is to advertise sites for public bidding, although some exceptions are made; for example, to accommodate businesses displaced by other park development.
Other public service facilities-notably camp grounds, where the demand has grown very greatly in recent years-are provided by the national parks administration. The policy here is simply to attempt to provide facilities as and where required, keeping in mind the importance of keeping inviolate the amenities which brought the visitors to the park in the first place.
I might remind hon. members here, Mr. Speaker, that the enormity of this problem and its importance can best be illustrated when I tell the house that the number of campers in our national parks has increased in the last ten years from 91,000 in 1952 to 634,000 in 1962.

What is the criterion under which an appointment of a postmaster is made in a revenue post office?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
The Postmaster General appoints revenue postmasters where the annual revenue of the office does not exceed $3,000. The criteria for selection are: (1) Canadian citizenship, (2) residence in the locality served by the post office, (3) adequate educational and other qualifications to perform the duties of the position, (4) ability to furnish accommodation, centrally located (5) priority to applicants who are entitled to the veterans preference and who are otherwise qualified as per 1, 2, 3, 4.
Appointments of postmasters in revenue post offices where the annual revenue exceeds $3,000 per annum are made by the civil service commission as the result of either closed or open competitions.
In the closed competitions, only postal employees may apply and the selection is based on the merit system. For the open competitions, in most cases, only residents of the area served by the post office may apply. However, if it is unlikely that a successful candidate can be found in the area served by the post office the competition would encompass a wider area. The appointment is made on the basis of merit and subject to the statutory preference for veterans.
On occasion there will be an assistant to the postmaster who will have sufficient

Questions
knowledge and experience to merit the appointment without the necessity of a formal competition. The deputy head will make this request to the commission which, if satisfied as to the equity of the case, will make the appointment subject to the appeal of other employees of the post office concerned.

The fate of French Canada
When he has considered all other problems which made the headlines during the election campaign, the Quebec voter is bound to ask: "What fate do the various parties calling on me to vote for them reserve for French Canada?"

What must be emphasized, however, is that the vast majority of French Canadians never will accept any solution where the bicultural character of Canada is overlooked, no matter how beneficial or immediately practical the solution might be. When we are fighting for a truly bicultural Canada, it is to ensure our very existence and collective development. And there is nothing to be gained, no reasonable compensation to be had in return which can justify a people to surrender those values.
Therefore, just before going to the polls, we must ask ourselves what promise and what dangers the coming election holds in store for us in that regard. The answer is not simple, far from it. One has the impression that the programs and positions of the respective parties give reason both for greater hopes and greater fears than ever for the French Canadians.
Let us look at the theoretical program and the concrete position of each party before the cultural reality of Canada.
There is no doubt that the Conservatives show, in this respect, the strangest contradictions. Never, in my opinion, has Mr. Dief-enbaker managed to utter one convincing word on that question. One feels that neither the prime minister nor his ministers have ever given it much thought. When they are asked for their opinion, they are almost proud of the fact that they have nothing to say on that matter. They waste no time in stating that the Conservative government has taken positive action instead of being satisfied with idle talk. And when they mention the measures taken by the Conservatives with regard to provincial autonomy, they are convincing. What is the required quorum, if any, to constitute a meeting of the federal cabinet?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
The cabinet is an informal body which discusses and decides questions of policy. Its organization and procedures are nowhere prescribed by law, but are matters for its own determination and are not normally disclosed. In its composition, however, the cabinet is identical with the committee of the privy council which exercises the right of the privy council for Canada "to aid and advise in the government of Canada" under section 11 of the British North America Act, 1867. It is the committee, then, and not the cabinet as such, which formally tenders advice to the Governor General when action by the governor in council is required. It has been the custom for many years that the committee of the council does not advise the Governor General to approve an order in council without the presence or concurrence of at least four ministers. This practice originated in the Queen's instructions to the Governor General at the time of confederation.
An order in council of 25th October, 1935, P.C. 3374, which has not since been varied or rescinded, states that "the quorum of the council being four, no submission for approval to the Governor General can be made with a less number than the quorum". This does not apply, however, to the deliberations and decisions of the cabinet as such, when it is not acting in its formal character as the committee.
Certain actions are taken by the Governor General, such as the appointment of ministers and the dissolution of parliament, on the basis of advice tendered by the Prime Minister alone, and no question of a quorum arises in such circumstances. It should be noted that the letters patent approved by the King in September 1947, and in effect since October of that year, constituting the office of Governor General of Canada state in paragraph II:
And we do hereby authorize and empower our Governor General, with the advice of our privy council for Canada or of any members thereof or individually, as the case requires, to exercise all powers and authorities lawfully belonging to us in respect of Canada, and for greater certainty but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing to do and execute, in the manner aforesaid, all things that may belong to his office and to the trust we have reposed in him according to the several powers and authorities granted or appointed him by virtue of The British North America Acts, 1867 to 1946 and the powers and authorities hereinafter conferred in these letters patent and in such commission as may be issued to him under our Great Seal of Canada and under such laws as are or may hereinafter be in force in Canada.

Therefore, in the absence of any agreement, it is my duty to deal with this request in the ordinary manner.
According to section (3) of standing order 26, when a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed is handed to the Speaker, he reads it out if he thinks it is in order and of urgent importance.
As hon. members know, it is well established in our practice that "urgency" within rule 26 does not apply to the matter itself but it means "urgency of debate".
Paragraph 3 of citation 100, Beauchesne's fourth edition reads as follows:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
As long ago as March 31, 1931, Mr. Speaker Black stated:
The reason for allowing such a motion is to afford members an opportunity of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance which they could do in no other way.
The matter proposed to be discussed today relates to the budget. As reported at page 1208 of Hansard of last Friday, the hon. Secretary of State announced that the budget debate would begin next Wednesday and that it was proposed that it should continue until completed.
When the budget debate is under way, it would seem to me that any question including any or all of the circumstances relating to the machinery followed in the preparation of the budget proposals would come within the ambit of debate. I suggest that it could not be otherwise.
In effect, then, there is a period of 48 hours between now and Wednesday-the period of ordinary notice as prescribed by standing order 41-before the rules and practice of the house will provide an opportunity to discuss every question relating to the preparation, presentation and/or implementation of the budget.
Under these circumstances, I must regretfully inform the house that I do not think that the hon. member's request is a matter of urgency of debate today within the meaning of standing order 26.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I took it upon myself to submit this notice of motion, because I believe that it is not only very important, but of extreme urgency. On the other hand, I think I shall find much goodwill among the Liberal members, as family allowances were part of their platform in the last general election. I trust that they will be only too happy at the opportunity I am giving them of voting for the fulfilment of their promises. Indeed, they are boasting, and rightly so, of having initiated that legislation. That is another argument against letting those allowances become inefficient.

Family Allowance Act
On the other hand, the Conservatives who were in opposition in 1944, when the legislation was enacted, all voted in favour of it and they too seemed to give their entire support to the basic principles of the measure. Those principles were very ably expounded by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King himself, as can be seen on page 5538 of Hansard dated July 28, 1944, and I shall quote his very words, because I agree with the principles he announced at that time:
By the measure on family allowances before this House of Commons today, we are seeking to further the law of peace, work and health.
It also should be said that the legislation was intended to cope with what actually was a social emergency; it had been shown up by the 1941 census, when it was discovered that 84 per cent of all children under 16 were dependant on only 19 per cent of the gainfully employed. And I have no reason to doubt that this percentage has changed now.
No better argument could be found in favour of legislation whose object was to provide our future citizens with care, food, clothes and adequate housing, as well as other necessities of life. As I said, I have no reason to believe that conditions are very much changed today and that the reasons which were valid at that time are no longer so, because those allowances have lost about half their value.
During that same speech he made on July 28, 1944 and quoting the great Pasteur, Mr. Mackenzie King stated:
-two contrary laws seem to be wrestling with each other nowadays: the one, a law of blood and of death, ever imagining new means of destruction and forcing nations to be constantly ready for the battlefield-the other, a law of peace, work, and health, ever evolving new means of delivering man from the scourges which beset him.
Which of these two laws shall ultimately prevail, God alone knows.
I think this is an opportunity for hon. members to show which of these two laws they favour.
Another reason to ask for a raise of family allowances is provided to us by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King himself when he stated, again in the same speech:
It starts with the natural resources which have been the gift of the Creator to mankind. The natural resources of any country have not been given to individuals; they have been given to the entire community, to the entire people. That, I think, we must realize as a fundamental truth, and all our efforts at the improvement of social and industrial conditions must be based upon that knowledge. But what has come to be the accepted view as we have developed the institution of private property? Not industry as existing for the good

of all-but industry as a means of private profit and gain. Are we then to throw aside all belief in the nature of private property because of some evils which have grown out of that system? Before we do so, we would do well to examine the position of private property as to what it means in the way of initiative, in development of resources and making them available for service and use, what it may also mean in the betterment of the masses.
Of course, I could quote many more passages from that speech in favour of family allowances but I shall merely read another paragraph because it disposes of the objections which could be put forward against the proposal now before the house. Indeed, Mr. Mackenzie King stated:
My own belief is that the measure itself is going to create so much in the way of employment that the national income will be so increased that we shall find it possible not only to have this class of social enactment self sustaining but be able as a consequence to have as well a reduction of debt and taxation.
Those are words which could fill with joy the heart of a good Social Crediter and would have no false ring in the mouth of our leader.
As for the Conservatives, I should like to recall what was their stand on that matter when this legislation was passed.
Mr. Diefenbaker rising in his place, as reported on page 5460 of Hansard for July 27, 1944 said:
With the objective provided for in this bill, there can be no disagreement; for if I understand it aright it means that through this measure an endeavour will be made to achieve equal opportunity, particularly for those in the lower income brackets, and to give many who today are denied freedom from fear and freedom from want the hope of something better in the future than this world and this country have seen before.
And further on, he quotes the report of the national resources development for 1943 which was placed before the president of the United States in January of that year. The report said:
There must be the fullest possible development of the human personality, in relation to the common good, in a framework of freedom and rights, of justice, liberty and equality and the consent of the governed, as the means of protecting justice, freedom and democracy.
We, in the parliaments of the empire, must recognize that the state must guarantee and underwrite equal access to security, to education, to nutrition and to health for all.
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as all those reasons I quoted as given by those hon. gentlemen were true and accurate in 1944, they are still true and accurate today for the simple reason that after creating family allowances, we have not been cautious enough to upgrade them

gradually to cope with the cost of living which continued to rise and is still rising nowadays. Furthermore, when we talk about doubling those allowances, we are not exaggerating, since countries much poorer than Canada, countries like France, for instance, actually give twice as much as we do.
In other words, due to inflation born of the present system, which is not a Social Credit system, family allowances have lost more than half their purchasing power; consequently they render slightly less than half the services they were meant to render, services we boasted about so much in 1944.
This is why, to widen their scope and to give them their true meaning, we first of all suggest that the present family allowances be doubled, in order to permit young people of this country who have the necessary aptitudes to go through the primary and high school systems and we suggest that family allowances be paid until age 20, provided the recipients stay in school and that after age 20, should our future citizens attend university, that they be paid an allowance in order that they may be enabled to attend university without always having to wonder what their parents are denying themselves and the other children in the family to enable them to stay in school. This would equalize opportunities for children of large families and others. This would also give our country an opportunity to take advantage of the many talents lost from day to day because parents do not have the means to keep their children at school, for everyone knows that children with the required intelligence and qualifications to benefit from higher education are not found solely in wealthy families.
It is for all the reasons I have already mentioned that I have the right to expect support from the two old line parties in this house, for I refuse to believe that the government will dare to break its word and try to shirk its responsibilities to the children of this country. To do that, it would have to go back on its word and prove disloyal to the memory of its most revered leaders, the Hon. Mr. King and the Hon. Mr. St. Laurent. That would be especially true in the case of the latter who, during the last years he was active in politics, had managed to become known as the great protector of Canadian children, so much so that in Quebec he is still called Uncle Louis.
It is hard to understand why the two old line parties have been so picayune in the matter of family allowances. They have recognized, up to a certain point at least, the principle that all social legislation should be geared to the cost of living. That principle is generally accepted in industry and it is 28902-5-80
Family Allowance Act
even considered natural that salaries should be geared to the cost of living.
But as far as family allowances are concerned, practically nothing has been done. Would it be that powerful secret forces are opposed to it because it would be to their advantage to destroy that main cell of the life of our nation which is the family? And please let us not hear again the old argument to the effect that we have no money, because there are many more appropriate areas where we could save for example, the field of nuclear weapons which will be obsolete in a year or two, and even the whole defence system where the Glassco report shows us cases of extensive and important waste.
I hope that members of all parties will vote for this motion so as to put a stop to what is said about them among the people. They find all the money they want when it is a matter of planning destruction and death but they cannot find any money when it comes to planning for life and construction.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Belanger) has three parts to it. First, it would double the present rate of family allowances. Second, it would authorize continuation of payment to 20 years of age while the child on whose behalf the allowance is paid is attending school. Third, the resolution proposes an increase in the allowance after the age of 20 if the recipient goes to university, to be in effect an anticipated salary during university attendance.
The hon. member for Charlevoix quoted very convincingly from the statement of the prime minister of the day at the time the allowances were first established. As was indicated, the measure was passed in August, 1944 and payments were made effective the first week in July, 1945. When the program began payments were made on behalf of 2,956,844 children at an annual rate of $232,700,000. For the present fiscal year the estimated expenditure is $542,900,000 on behalf of close to 6,700,000 children. Payments are made on behalf of more than one third of the population of Canada who are within the age group up to 16 years of age.
When the program was first introduced the payments were on a graduated scale starting with $5 a month up to 6 years of age, then $6 up to 9 years of age, $7 up to 12 years of age and $8 between the years of 13 to 15 inclusive. At that time the rates were reduced in the case of large families. For the fifth child $1 less was paid, for the sixth child $2 less, for the seventh child $2 less and for the eighth child $3 less. The changes

Family Allowance Act
which were made in 1949 abolished this discrimination against larger families which it weis difficult, it is true, to justify.
In 1957 further changes were introduced and at the present time the rates are $6 a month for children who have not yet attained their tenth birthday and $8 a month for children between their tenth Eind sixteenth birthdays. Estimates for the 1963-64 fiscal year show an increase of not quite $11 million, or of the order of 2 per cent of what was paid before. For previous years the rate of growth of our child population has been in excess of this percentage.

If the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) would pay attention he might ascertain my purpose is to indicate the grounds that were put forward by the earliest proponents of family allowance, what they hoped to achieve by such measures. We, on this side of the house, were responsible for putting this legislation on the statute books. To suggest that we are in any way unsympathetic towards this is a gross distortion. We know what the purpose of the family allowance program is. There will be a measure put before this house which will deal, in part, with the resolution which the hon. member has in mind. I hope that by the time I am through with my remarks the hon. member will have some second thoughts concerning some aspects of the resolution.
The question of the development of a wage policy, I said, was one of the grounds used in the debate on this issue and was one to which the government of the day gave a good deal of attention. This was also a measure

to stimulate post-war prosperity in the tor-ties, toward the end of the war. The advisers of the government were very much concerned with a measure which would provide a large amount of consumer purchasing power in the anticipated slackening off which would be part of the story of the adjustment from wartime to peacetime. The family allowance measure was put forward with the full support of the fiscal advisers of the government who felt it was an appropriate piece of legislation for Canada at that time.
The third reason which is often advanced, and which I do not think carries as much weight with us, is the suggestion that this is a positive instrument of population or demographic policy. In many parts of the world this is true. Many countries have adopted family allowance measures with a very different approach from the Canadian approach. They feel in France, for example, that an equalization fund for private employers should have a set objective to build up family allowances to something like 25 per cent of wages. Under those circumstances, there is some evidence that family allowance policy has had some effect upon family formation.
People who have studied our program, or attempted to draw comparisons with other parts of the world, had concluded that our program has had no significant effect upon the Canadian birth rate or family formation. For instance, our neighbour to the south does not have a family allowance program. During the ten years subsequent to 1946, the birth rate per thousand in Canada rose 10.4 points and in the United States 12.4 points. True it rose from a lower base in the United States in the first instance. The general picture of demographic trends and those who have advanced demographic purposes for family allowance legislation, usually suggest that in the case of a country such as Canada the most significant factors are the general level of employment and income. Thus, the effects are very much greater than anything that can be traced to family allowance purposes.
The resolution, Mr. Speaker, I think has to stand on the basic purposes for which it was advanced by the government of the day. This relates to a measure of social justice for which we all have the very greatest sympathy. I listened to the hon. member for Charlevoix when he started to quote the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King in the debate, and to suggest correctly that 84 per cent of the children were supported by 19 per cent of the wage earners, one fifth of the wage earners of the country. This is a proportion which seems to be borne out in widely different circumstances and cultures. The basic inequality of such a thing is the real reason

Family Allowance Act
for family allowances. They are, fundamentally, an attack on poverty which is associated with large families. They represent a measure of equality of opportunity for Canadian children, and under such circumstances they have been the bulwark, fundamentally, of our entire structure of social security.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I said the resolution had three arms to it and I have indicated the general grounds which the measure was implemented and defended not only in Canada but in other parts of the world. I give full credit to the people who have consistently taken an interest in this legislation, an interest that goes beyond the superficial. However, we must bear in mind that the question of the extension of family allowances to meet the purpose of higher education calls for further examination.
Our party is committed to extending family allowances to children at school to the age of 18 years. At the appropriate time, I am sure legislation will be brought before this house to implement the commitment which we firmly made during the course of the election campaign. However, I presume one of the purposes of this measure would be to extend family allowances and make them the basis of a salary for students attending university. It is significant that in one of the early literature or the statements made at the time was there such a purpose indicated. Our party is on the record as supporting a program of national scholarships, which I am certain is a more logical, more satisfactory approach towards permitting worthy students of modest circumstances to achieve a higher education. I do not believe that the extension of the family allowance to $18 per month is going to give the person attending university a large salary. I do not believe the hon. member seriously believes for one minute this sum would be adequate for the purpose which the hon. member has outlined.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have an aspect of this matter which I am sure the mover of the resolution will want to consider very carefully. We have had a budget placed before this house on which there will be a debate in the near future. We noted that budgetary expenditures were in the area of $6,500 million. I have indicated that the estimated costs of the family allowances for the present year exceed $530 million. The effect of the proposed measure would be to add over $530 million to the budget deficit which would have to be faced by this house. The hon. member has indicated that he is in favour of economy in many other areas of government operation. I wonder if he has given thought to the implications of continuing the federal government in the field of fiscal relations to this magnitude at a time when a question has

Family Allowance Act
been raised concerning the appropriate share of various tax fields for the provincial, municipal and federal authorities.
Certainly, the raising of this sum of money through federal taxation, and the spending of it in the form in which family allowances are now spent, would have some interesting redistribution effects. Very few people have studied the regional effects of the redistribution of family allowances. One of the gentlemen who did attempt a very good study is the man to whom I referred earlier, the present deputy minister of national welfare. In an article published in International Labour Review for March, 1957, he cited some facts to which I should like to refer.
For the fiscal year 1954-55 the four Atlantic provinces provided 3.8 per cent of the direct tax revenues of the federal authority and received 12.8 per cent of the family allowance payments. The prairie provinces were the source of 11.4 per cent of direct tax revenues and received 17.7 per cent of family allowance payments. The province of Quebec was the source of 26.1 per cent of direct tax revenues and received 31.7 per cent of the family allowance payments. B.C. was the source of 9.6 per cent direct tax revenues and received 7.5 per cent of family allowance payments. Ontario was the source of 49 per cent direct tax revenues and received 30.2 per cent of family allowance payments.
I think there is a great deal of evidence that this redistribution is a highly desirable form of income redistribution. It goes from the wealthy areas to those with less capacity to support the general level of welfare and educational services, and to provide such basic things as food, clothing and shelter. This is one of the very good aspects of the program.
The program uses the federal authority directly as a source of raising funds and dispensing funds, and when we come to look at the redistribution within families we find some very interesting things. The study to which I refer covered the year ending August 31, 1948 and I have been unable to find any subsequent studies. In fact I think it is time another was undertaken, but the study showed that for all families receiving family allowances the allowances amounted to 4.9 per cent of net income.
Families with three or more children, and with incomes below $3,000, benefited to the greatest extent. Generally speaking the real impact of the family allowances program is found on families earning more than $3,000 and with no more than three children, and here the percentages of income tend to become significant. In the case of families with five and more children, family allowances were something like 12.8 per cent of family income.

This is a very significant redistribution measure, and when we review the program today I think we recognize that the impact that was feared in 1944 by two of the three major organized labour bodies has not come to pass.
There is a wide degree of support, almost unanimous, from all parties to the program. The program itself is basically a measure of social justice-

I only wish to say a few words on this motion and to congratulate the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Belanger) for bringing it forward. During the recent election campaign all political parties supported the idea of supplying more equal distribution of wealth through social justice, or whatever term one wishes to call it. The matter of family allowances was also supported by all parties.
Like the speaker immediately preceding me I was surprised to see this was omitted from the budget, and unlike some of the previous speakers I am not so convinced that the government will introduce measures along this line, unless it is prodded into doing so. I have always felt family allowances were to provide for the education of young children, and when the act was originally introduced the age of 16 years was the average age at which children finished their education and went to work. However, we have moved very rapidly in the educational field, and 16 years is no longer the age at which children go to work. In many cases their education continues for another four or five years, and rather than stipulate the age of 20 I believe these allowances should be continued to the age of 21.
I have children in that category myself and I have found no lessening of their expenses after the age of 16 years. As a matter of fact it seems to be more expensive to outfit children after the age of 16; and so not only do I think the age limit should be extended but payments should be on a graduated scale, rising with the age of the recipient.
The question of raising the allowance, or doubling it, is one for the house or a committee of the house to discuss, but no matter what decision is reached I believe we should include a new provision gearing family allowances to the cost of living so that we will not continuously have to raise this matter in parliament. The country has watched the gymnastics that have taken place in social security, particularly in relation to old age pensions, with one political party trying to outdo another. I only hope this does not happen in the field of family allowances, and that allowances will be brought into line with the purchasing power that was originally intended. That would probably increase them
Family Allowance Act
by at least 50 per cent, and with the new provision that they be geared to the cost of living they can be taken out of the realm of political promises at election time.
I am not too well informed as to what has been done in other countries or in what way social security programs have been applied relating to this matter of student salaries. To my mind this is a new area and is one which I think many people in Canada in the educational field would want to consider before we adopted in a family allowance bill. There would probably be those who would want to discuss the constitutionality of this problem. I am quite sure there would be some who would think that if the federal government were to pay a salary to students attending university, some of the provincial autonomy in the field of education would be superimposed on the federal government. I am not sure that this is true, but I think there are those who would argue this way. This might be a limitation to our passing an increase in family allowances at this time, and I hope the mover of the resolution will indicate either that this question will be considered or he is willing to consider an amendment that would allow us at another time to discuss the question separately from family allowances.
I believe family allowances have been used to great advantage by Canadian families. I know personally of hundreds and hundreds of cases where children who are now attending school would not have been able to do so if it were not for the limited assistance that is given by the family allowance. In many cases this amounts to a very large portion of the cash income of the family. I believe this measure has served a need and that governments are being very slow in waiting for the push that is sometimes given by elections in regard to legislating family allowance increases. I hope the government will consider sending this subject to a committee, as they have other subjects, where it can be discussed. The merits of the two proposals, which are fairly separate in my opinion, could be discussed in committee. There would then be no delay in the implementing of a large increase in the family allowance and the extension of that allowance to take into consideration the changes which have been made in our educational system in allowing our children a longer period of education before they enter the labour market.

Mr. Speaker, before making a few remarks about this motion, I wish to point out how unfortunate it is that some members take part in the debate on such an important matter solely to make political capital.

Family Allowance Act
I am of the opinion that an act should be adopted to make it impossible to treat in such a way social legislation.
Mr. Speaker, it must be admitted that the Family Allowances Act is certainly, and we are all agreed on that, one of the best pieces of social legislation ever passed by the house.
I do not want to take up the valuable time of the house to praise the benefits of that act. I only want to make humble suggestions which, if they were implemented, would make this act much more effective and more profitable for the many families who benefit from it.
At the end of March 1962, 2,649,317 families were in receipt of family allowances for 6,562,287 children, that is for more than a third of the total population of Canada. Net payments for the year were $520,781,193.
In actual fact, what did the Family Allowances Act cost the country the amount of $520,781,193 during the fiscal year ended March 1962?
No, Mr. Speaker, because even though that sum was paid through the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of National Revenue, by virtue of the same act, has collected many thousand dollars, the exact amount being impossible to estimate. This statement may astonish many members but you will easily understand what I mean after the following explanations.
On page 2 of the income tax return T-l, paragraph 2, we can read: Exemption for children qualified for family allowances- $300, and for each child not qualified for family allowances-$550.
If you figure it out, here are the results you will get. A person with an annual income of $3,000 and who has a child is entitled to an exemption of $2,350 if the child is eligible for family allowances; so his taxable income will be $650, which represents an income tax payment of $80. If the child were not qualified for family allowances, his exemption would then amount to $2,550 and his taxable income would be $450; consequently, the amount he would have to pay as income tax would be $56, that is $24 he must pay as additional income tax because he receives $72 in family allowances. We may conclude that that person must pay as income tax a third of the amount received in family allowances.
We see also that with an income of $5,000, a family of four children will receive $288 in family allowances, but the father will have to pay $113 more in income tax, which means

that the family allowances in this case come to $175 for the year. So, for each child, the government does not grant $6, but in fact $3.60 a month.
Let us consider the case of a father of eight with an annual income of $8,000. Because he receives an amount of $648 in family allowances, instead of paying $182 in income tax, he will have to pay the Department of National Revenue the amount of $442, that is a difference of $260 in additional income tax.
And the same arithmetic can be repeated for the 2,649,317 families receiving family allowances.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday

Inquiries of the Ministry I promised to give an answer today to a question put by the hon. member for Skeena on June 5, 1963, about the return of documents such as landing papers, passports and citizenship certificates seized in the case of Chinese people who are alleged to have entered Canada illegally.
There are two types of occasions on which documents have been or are obtained either by officers of the R.C.M.P. or immigration officers in matters of illegal Chinese immigration. First, there are the cases of direct investigation by the R.C.M.P. of illegal immigration activities, such as the one made some three years ago. I am advised that the documents seized on these occasions have been seized in each case under the authority of search warrants and that they have been or are returned to the persons from whom they were taken on completion of the R.C.M.P. investigation.
Then there are the occasions when an individual has made or has indicated an intention to make a statement as to his identity to an immigration officer. On these occasions such documents as landing cards, citizenship certificates and passports are retained from the immigrant by the immigration officer. They are not returned to him but are sent to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration for retention pending the adjustment of status. There is, of course, no point in leaving these documents in the possession of these immigrants in the meantime, inasmuch as the status purported to be certified by them is false. However, once the immigrant's status has been adjusted these documents are reissued under the changed identity and remitted to the immigrant.
If my hon. friend will let me have the name of any Chinese whose documents have been taken from him and not returned or replaced, I shall certainly look into this.

The house resumed from Friday, June 14, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Gordon-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to promote increased employment in Canada by the provision of financial assistance by way of loans to municipalities, the object of such loans being to enable municipalities to augment or accelerate their capital works programs subject to the approval of the provinces concerned: and for this purpose to provide a special fund in a consolidated revenue fund not exceeding four hundred million dollars to be available for the making of loans to municipalities and certain other municipal authorities for specific municipal capital works projects: to establish a municipal development and loan board to administer the fund so provided; to authorize the acceptance of municipal debentures for any loans so made; to authorize a measure of forgiveness in respect of any loans so made, depending upon the date of completion of the projects for 28902-5-81i
17, 1963	1259
Municipal Development and Loan Board which such loans are made; and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO PUT QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
In rising to speak on this resolution, I do so with some hesitation because of the extremely active debate which has ranged in this house for the last day or so as a result of the irregularities in the preparation of the budget. One's mind has wandered far, but I shall endeavour to get back to this resolution dealing with loans to municipalities. I noticed that the fund will be established out of the consolidated revenue fund and will be $400 million. The resolution proclaimed that the main objective of this measure was to increase employment. I must say that I am doubtful the objective will be achieved, and I will explain my reasons for this as I go along.
First of all, there has been a limitation placed on the use of this money. The minister stated that he estimated this measure might cover half the normal borrowings of the municipalities and might cover two thirds of the cost of the projects. He went on to explain the rate of interest and the forgiveness features.
In so far as the $400 million is concerned, the other night it was pointed out that in the last five years the previous government made $900 million available to the municipalities through the winter works program.
This was directly for use during winter time when unemployment is highest, but here are $400 million to be spread over three years and to be used any time of the year. This is one of the basic differences.
The last time something like this was attempted was in 1938 when an act was passed called the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. Under it money was to be lent at 2 per cent interest, and there was a definite regulation clause written into the act dealing with the amount of money that could be lent to any particular municipality. It may be such a provision will be written into the bill that will follow this resolution. Section 6 of the 1938 act stipulated that loans to municipalities should relate to the percentage their populations bore to the population of the country, but I fear that under this legislation loans will be made on a wide open basis to the larger municipalities, and that they will gobble up the greatest part of the $400 million, possibly within the first year.
Hon. members should keep those remarks in mind, and should also consider what has taken place here during the last couple of days with the government showing a definite favouritism to Toronto, Bay street interests,
1260	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board and to investment brokers. It is quite conceivable that most of this fund will be channelled into the larger centres. This is one of the greatest fears I have in regard to the proposed bill.
I believe the money should be lent on a per capita basis, giving each municipality a chance to borrow for projects which would give a long term return. To set up a municipal loan fund for three years is not enough. It cannot possibly begin to become a revolving fund in any sense of the term because most municipal loans are taken out for 20, 25 or 30 years. I might add that the interest rate is not particularly appealing either.
I hope the forgiveness clause in the proposed bill will be as good as the forgiveness clause with regard to sewerage projects undertaken under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation during recent years, when 25 per cent was written off if capital works projects were undertaken within a specified time.
These are things which should be considered with regard to this municipal loan fund before it is held up to mayors, reeves and councillors all across the country as the answer to their hopes and prayers for money to develop their municipalities. We in the province of Alberta do not look forward to this fund with any real interest because we have one great fear that loans may be made without any great deal of judgment with regard to their efficiency. By that I mean there is no real objection towards making a 20 year loan to a municipality for a capital works project that will continue to give employment, but there is towards making loans for structures which will be outdated within that time and will require to be replaced by more modern structures before the original loans are written off.
Municipalities in Alberta are also notable for the heavy debt load they carry already, and this loan fund cannot be held up as the answer to their hopes. This subject has been dealt with already during the debate and I do not want to put the figures on record another time; but what the municipalities need are more generous grants towards capital works projects, and not necessarily more loans which will place them further and further in debt.
The Alberta legislature has set up the Alberta Finance Corporation which makes loans to municipalities. When it was first set up it made loans at 2.5 per cent interest. Now the interest is up to 4.5 per cent, and even 5 per cent in many cases. Municipalities in Alberta have taken great advantage of this act and many improvements have been made in both the smaller and larger centres.


One principal necessity is for government at all levels to look ahead and plan ahead in the financing of capital works projects. Municipalities must gauge with reasonable accuracy their estimated population growth before determining the need for loans. This holds true for municipalities, towns and cities, and they must be able to gauge their needs 10 and 20 years from now.
While I hesitate to agree that this loan will solve the unemployment problem, I think that loans made to municipalities for the construction of works which will continue to create employment in the years ahead would be much more beneficial than undertaking projects which provide jobs while they are being built, but after they are completed do not provide any more jobs. With the limiting factors placed upon loans under the proposed legislation, no loans will be made to municipalities for sewerage, water, and many other types of projects which would be more beneficial and helpful in curing unemployment.
We have heard considerable talk about whether a municipal loan fund should be established out of the consolidated revenue fund or as an arm of the Bank of Canada. I do not think it makes any difference, but we have to have close co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal governments because the provinces, through their direction of road programs and water development projects can control and regulate the growth of municipalities, towns and cities. For that reason I think the federal government in setting up the proposed board should keep close liaison with the provincial authorities.
That is an important point to consider at this time because we have just heard an answer on orders of the day to the effect that one of the provinces has asked the government to slow up, and perhaps not to pass the bill that will spring out of the resolution we are now debating, until after the provincial governments meet in August. That is important to consider because the success of the proposed act will be based upon the co-operation achieved between the federal, provincial and municipal governments.
The remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer, with regard to the loan board which it is proposed to establish, were very interesting. He said there were three types of capital available to municipalities, namely tax capital, commercial capital and social capital, and he implied that social capital was the same thing as social credit. As I am from Alberta I was glad at least to find out what social credit was; apparently it is social capital. "Social capital" is a nice phrase. I do not know who first coined it

The hon. member talks about votes being counted. That is fine. I can remember some votes being counted in the constituency of Red Deer not so long ago. The hon. member must have found out a lot of things that particular night too.
On this point it is interesting to bring to the attention of the committee, with regard to social capital and municipal loans, that on February 28, 1961 a similar debate took place in the Alberta legislature. That legislature was at the time debating the question of whether or not they should ask the federal
17, 1963	1261
Municipal Development and Loan Board government to set up a municipal loan fund. Mr. Manning, the premier of the province, entered the debate for the first time in the session and explained that a distinction should be drawn between social capital and those funds belonging to private individuals or corporations. I would like his government to produce a Hansard so that, rather than reading a report on the debate, I would be able to follow him verbatim and perhaps get a better idea of just what is meant by social capital as applied to municipalities.
Premier Manning went on to say that this social capital should be made available to municipalities to borrow at the going rate of interest. This is the premier of the Social Credit government in Alberta talking. He said they must expect to pay the going rate of interest. That is an interesting remark coming from a party which believes in no interest rates, or interest rates which are not greater than the cost of administering the loan. He suggests that a bank be set up under the Bank of Canada, something similar to that which the hon. member for Red Deer suggested in the debate on June 14. He also admitted, and I think this is very interesting, that if the money is made available through the Bank of Canada-I suppose he did not like to use the phrase "print it", but I suppose this is what he implied-that the plan would produce inflationary pressures. This is also quite an admission coming from the Social Credit group which over the years has said that the money supply has nothing to do with inflation. It is quite an admission coming from the premier of that province, who admitted that such a plan would produce inflationary pressures. He suggested that the Bank of Canada could control this by increasing the percentage of cash chartered banks must have on deposit in proportion to the amount on loan. This was his explanation of how inflation could be controlled, by making more money available from social capital and limiting the amount of money available through commercial channels such as the chartered banks. This would be the result of this action, to increase the percentage of cash the chartered banks must have on deposit in proportion to the amount on loan. This would be the security held against the amount loaned. This again, is a surprising thing coming from a party which advocates, and advocated on June 14, that this was one type of capital which should be expanded in order to promote free enterprise. How can you promote free enterprise by limiting commercial capital? Is that promoting free enterprise? I hardly think so. On one hand they want to increase social capital
1262	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and, Loan Board and on the other they want to limit commercial capital and promote free enterprise. This is an impossibility.

speechtext:
I would like to do just that and I would like the hon. member for Red Deer to count the votes in the riding of Red Deer tonight. But I realize, Mr. Chairman, that these hecklers are drawing me away from the subject under discussion and I want to get back to it. I think one of the important things we must bear in mind is that loans should be made for no longer than the useful life of the project. If the credit is extended beyond the useful life of the project it is a very inefficient type of loan. It is an inefficient type of loan because it will cost the municipality far more money than the interest rate; it will cost three or four times the amount of the interest rate. The hon. member for Red Deer referred to several projects which were constructed for 50 years -and we have read about these-where the loan has recently been paid off, long after the project had gone. In many cases they had been torn up years ago. I think this must be guarded against in making freer capital available to municipalities instead of, to quote the hon. member for Red Deer again, rubbing liniment on an ache or pain, and continuing the life of the ache or pain. Such a remedy might eventually do more harm than good. Applied in another way, in the field of finance, it might eventually cripple the whole provincial tax structure.
This is one of the great dangers with which the municipalities of Alberta are faced today. There is a danger that their tax structure will be crippled because of the high municipal debts in the province. In no province in Canada is municipal debt higher than it is in Alberta; there is no province where land taxes are as high as they are in Alberta. This is because money has been made available to the municipalities through loans, but not enough has been made available by means of grants. The former federal government made grants of money to the provinces in larger amounts, by way of direct grants, than ever before. Something like $3.6 billion was made available to the provinces across


Canada during the last five years so that they might better meet their requirements.
We in this house all realize that the municipalities have, as their main sources of revenue, the taxes imposed on property and on land. It is true that some provincial governments make grants available to the municipalities out of revenue from sales taxes, gasoline taxes and so on. But by far the greatest amount of their revenue comes from land taxes. As a farmer, and as one who is, possibly, closer to the land than some others in this house, I realize the danger which the municipalities across Canada are facing when they must impose high rates of taxation in order to meet the cost of their municipal borrowing. This is why great care must be taken in applying for these loans. It is well and good for the government to say it intends to pour out money in order to do away with unemployment.

speechtext:
Nothing pleases a speaker more than to know people are listening to him, and I am glad members opposite have been paying attention to what I have been saying. It does my heart good. I may go on for 20 minutes longer.
I am aware that the mayors and municipalities at their meeting in Toronto recently wanted a municipal fund set up from which they could borrow money. But I wish to give this warning and say that such a fund may not be the answer to their desires. If not properly used, it may lead them further into debt. And who would have to pay this debt? The land owners throughout Canada would have to do so, whether they own property in a city or a farm in the province of Alberta. It would come from taxes on land, because this is where the municipalities acquire the greatest part of their revenue.
Lest there be any doubt about it, let me say that I am in favour of the bill, with certain reservations as to how the loans should be made. I am against the limitations placed on the use of this fund because they seem to

me to be applied in such a way as to encourage capital projects which will not provide tor continuous employment. Jobs will be produced, it is true, while the capital projects are being built, but the money invested will not continue to produce jobs in the years ahead. If loans were made available in respect of water development, for example, there would be a continuous multiciplicity of jobs becoming available each year as a result of the initial capital expenditure. I know of many municipalities in my constituency which are constantly handicapped by the lack of ample water supplies and I wonder why loans in connection with water development projects could not be made available under this scheme.
Without doubt, loans to municipalities would help in getting them over the hump. But loans should be made in respect of projects capable of creating jobs as a result of which more money would flow into the coffers of the municipality concerned. I do not want to see this $400 millions lent out and spent on projects for capital works which would, in the end, increase government employment, for example. We all realize at one time or another that, to an extent, we are serving the people; we are working for the people. But the people are paying the cost of this administration, so we do not want the cost of administration of government to increase, whether municipally, federally, or provincially. That is why I say this fund must be spent in such a way that eventually more money will go back to municipal coffers.
I have tried to deal with some of the reservations I feel with regard to this loan project. I should like to deal with one more which particularly affects the smaller municipalities across Canada. This is the fear of being left completely out of participation in this $400 millions which is to be made available. They are in fear that the Bay street interests of the present government may control and funnel this $400 millions into the larger cities throughout the country and that the smaller rural municipalities will have none of it made available to them for the betterment of life in their areas. I hope the bill when drafted contains a provision similar to that which was written into the act to assist municipalities which was drawn up in 1938. I am told this measure was in effect only until 1939 when it got too hot for the government of that day to handle. I should like to see the present measure enjoy a longer life, longer even than three years, and make money available on a per capita basis to municipalities across Canada.

speechtext:
I do not intend at this time to speak at length or in detail on the provisions
17, 1963	1263
Municipal Development and Loan Board of the municipal loan and development bill. The resolution placed on the order paper on May 20 stated the main purpose of the statute and indicated some of its principal features.
In my earlier remarks to the committee I affirmed the intention of the loan program to stimulate the economy and provide new jobs while at the same time assisting municipalities to construct basic capital facilities. In the debate on the resolution so far questions have arisen with respect to the detailed operation of the program. For the most part, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that further discussion on matters of this kind can be carried on more usefully perhaps after hon. members have had the chance to read the bill itself. I think it is rather difficult for hon. members to discuss the bill when they have not seen it, although I must say they have been doing very well under this handicap. In many instances answers to the questions which have been raised will be found in the provisions of the bill when it comes before the committee. However, in the course of the debate a few points of a more general nature arose on which I should like to comment now.
Let me first refer to the place of the proposed municipal loans programs in the over-all policies of economic expansion and new employment being developed by this government. The municipal loan program constitutes action designed to produce new jobs in the intermediate term. Among other measures announced by my colleague last week, were some designed for short term effects while others are intended to have their major impact over a longer period of years. All are integral parts of a national program of action. Each has its essential place in a plan of national development. The municipal loans in particular will have significant effects this winter-that is, of course, if the legislation is passed in time-and major effects in the two years following. They thus play an important role in the intermediate term.
The authorized amount of the program is $400 million-or that is what is being asked for. If fully utilized it will assist in the construction of some $600 million worth of additional municipal projects. Some hon. members have suggested that this amount seems small in view of the capital needs of the municipalities. The government does not hold this view. These are large sums, Mr. Chairman, and when we take into account the time of nearly three years, together with the range of eligible projects and the fact that the loans are to be applied to additional projects, then the $600 million of assisted projects constitutes a very substantial effort on the part of the municipalities.
1264	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board
In this respect I would ask hon. members to consider for the moment the demand for sewage treatment loans under the National Housing Act. This program has been in effect now for two and a half years. It has an authorized limit of $200 million. What has been the experience under that program? As of June 7, 1963 some 442 loans were made aggregating $100,285,000. Thus almost $100 million of loans remain available after two and a half years of operation. Against this amount there are now outstanding 14 applications aggregating approximately $4 million. The rate of utilization of this program may give some hon. members assurances as to the adequacy of the proposed new program, and I respectfully ask hon members to reserve judgment as to its scope until they have seen the bill. They can then relate it to the other programs being developed under the National Housing Act. For some of these older programs the government intends to propose amendments and improvements.
I also want to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that loans will be available to all municipalities, large and small. Indeed, it is to be expected that the smaller municipalities will participate fully in the new program. The eligible projects are such that they will find ample opportunity to participate. Once again, if I may say so, this has been the experience under the sewage loan program, where, for example, more than one fifth of the loans were made to small communities in Saskatchewan. Loans to municipalities of all sizes were made throughout the country and there is every reason to expect that a similar pattern will emerge under the proposed municipal loans plan.
The other night, Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition asked whether the proposed program of municipal loans had been placed before the provinces before being presented to the house. This has not been done. It is the government's view that it is the right of parliament to have first opportunity of discussing this plan on the resolution stage, and then when parliament has expressed its views it will be appropriate to discuss the plan with the provincial authorities. As I have indicated, the proposed loan plan has been developed with full regard for the constitutional rights of the provinces.

No, Mr. Chairman, and if the hon. member will allow me to finish what I


was about to come to, I think it will be quite clear to him. As I have indicated, the proposed loan plan has been developed with full regard for the constitutional rights of the provinces. When hon. members see the proposed legislation I am sure they will appreciate that the program cannot proceed and that loans cannot be made until appropriate procedures have been discussed and worked out with the provinces. Loan applications must not only be approved by the provinces; they must also be transmitted by the provinces to the proposed loan board. The cooperation of the provinces will thus be required and they will be consulted. The government is confident, Mr. Chairman, that the same co-operation which has existed under past and similar programs will continue under the proposed plan. I repeat, however, that the government's position in this matter is that parliament's views should first be ascertained. Approval of the plans should first be sought in the house and this is the course we propose to follow.
Let me point out that the course proposed is not an unusual one. Indeed, there are many precedents. Several of these relate to the procedures followed by the previous government. Let me cite the sewage loan program under part VI B of the National Housing Act initiated by the previous government in 1960 without, to the best of my knowledge, any prior consultation with the provinces of the kind suggested the other evening by the Leader of the Opposition. This program broke new ground in the field of assistance to municipalities by way of loans, but as I say I believe there was no prior consultation. A similar course was followed, so far as I am aware, in the case of the winter works incentive program. Here was a program of grants to municipalities decided upon by the government of the day without prior consultation with the provinces. The same was true, I understand, with the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act passed by this parliament under the former government, but before consultations took place with the provinces who were vitally affected.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the course we propose to follow is clearly not a departure from established practice. I noted with interest the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition which appear on page 892 of Hansard, where he stated that his reading suggests to him that:
-public works have been ineffective as a means of meeting unemployment on any economical basis or standard, the cost is too great, and they do not provide jobs.
This is not the economic philosophy of this government and I doubt that it will appeal to members of the committee. We on this

side of the house are confident that the proposed plan will produce many thousands of new jobs and we have every confidence that it will operate with the co-operation of the provinces and within the framework of the constitution. To that end, Mr. Chairman, I ask the co-operation of members of the committee in expediting passage of the proposed legislation.
