speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance in his brief outline has cleared up some of the points I had in mind in rising to speak, so as a result my speech will be much shorter. However, he still has not established in my mind that this plan is exactly what the municipalities desire and expect from the government, I am not an expert in municipal finance or in administration, but one does not have to be an expert in these matters to see that the program oulined in the resolution before us does not meet the present requirements of the municipalities and certainly does not provide for their future plans.
Like other speakers I am in agreement with the principle of a municipal loan fund, but the proposed loan arrangement does not come near fulfilling the great Liberal promises in the last election campaign. There are very few signs of the much-publicized, bold, imaginative program to end unemployment. The Leader of the Opposition emphasized the weaknesses and shortcomings of this municipal loan plan and other speakers have also dealt with particular points. As I said, the Minister of Finance has dealt with some of these points so that I do not need to repeat them now, but they will certainly be brought up again when the bill is considered in detail.
The resolution states that this is a measure to promote increased employment in Canada. We all agree with this objective, although we do not think that this plan will meet that objective. The objective of meeting the problem of unemployment is an objective with regard to which the former government had made and was continuing to make remarkable progress when its program of national development was obstructed by the opposition and the government was voted out of office.
I am sure we all agree that a municipal loan fund is necessary. Such a fund has been requested by the municipalities, as has been brought out by other speakers. But lending $400 million over the next three years to municipalities cannot be regarded as the full answer to their needs. A loan fund of $400 million seems like a tremendous sum and it is a tremendous amount especially when, as our leader pointed out, there is no indication just where or how the government intends to obtain this money.
17, 1963	1265
Municipal Development and Loan Board
How far will $400 million go in fulfilling the government's promise of full employment especially when, as other speakers have pointed out, the government gives with one hand and takes away with the other hand? In connection with the matter of giving and at the same time taking back I am thinking of the imposition by the budget of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. I am not sure how many hundreds of millions of dollars the Minister of Finance expects to receive from the 11 per cent tax on building materials but I imagine it will take a large slice out of the $400 million set aside for municipal programs.
What I am attempting to point out is that the larger part of any loan to a municipality under this program will have to be spent on building materials, leaving only a smaller portion of the loan for employment payrolls. The production of the building materials will, of course, provide jobs but I am thinking of smaller centres where building materials are not produced locally. In these smaller centres the increased building costs already imposed by the new government which has been in office for less than 60 days will do little to encourage or help building by municipalities.
There is another aspect of the proposed loan fund which will be of common concern to smaller centres. It has been made clear by the government that the fund will not be made available for the construction of hospitals, schools, university buildings or sewage systems. In the smaller centres the exclusion of these items will leave very little in the way of capital works that can be undertaken. As has been pointed out by other speakers, especially by the hon. member for Acadia, this means that the larger centres will receive nearly all the benefit from the proposed loans. This was indicated by the headlines in a Toronto paper following the announcement of this program. There were several stories about major projects in Toronto that would likely be eligible for loans from the $400 million fund. The cost of these proposed projects would take almost one third of the entire loan fund.
I am not blaming Toronto for trying to get all it can. We all know the city's reputation and the name it has been given because of its acquisitive habits. What I am trying to point out to the government, as others have pointed out, is that there must be some limit on what one city or one area can receive. I hope this will be made clear in the bill when it comes before us for consideration. I know the Minister of Finance touched on the subject but I think it should be brought out in more detail and, as the hon. member for Acadia said, there should be a definite limit
1266	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board on the amount for any one centre. I have no idea what plans the municipalities in my area have but I am sure they will want their share and I am here to see that they get their share, and that all the money does not go to the large centres.
The Leader of the Opposition pointed out the difficulties likely to arise in securing dominion-provincial agreement with regard to the administration of the loan fund. These difficulties need not be repeated now. Perhaps I could ask the government one question with regard to the provinces. I know that some of the provinces have municipal loan arrangements of their own, but does this particular loan program envisage any contribution to the municipalities from the provincial governments? I am thinking of the winter works program of the former government under which Ottawa paid 50 per cent of the labour costs and the provincial governments paid 25 per cent. Under the former government there was a scheme of technical and vocational training, and Ottawa paid 75 per cent of the building cost and the province 25 per cent. I could cite another example from my own province of Saskatchewan. Ottawa is paying 75 per cent of the cost of constructing the south Saskatchewan dam and the provincial government is paying 25 per cent. Will there be provisions under which the provincial governments will participate in these municipal loans?
One reason for asking this question, Mr. Chairman, is the surplus of nearly $10 million reported by the Saskatchewan government for the last fiscal year. While the municipalities were cutting their works programs in an attempt to balance their budgets, the Saskatchewan government built up a surplus of nearly $10 million. I do not believe the government at Regina should take such pride in a budget surplus when this $10 million could have been used to help the municipalities.
This is not the whole story, Mr. Chairman, with regard to this surplus. The Saskatchewan government received from Ottawa, among other items, and I am not going to mention them all, over $30 million under certain tax sharing agreements, subsidies and so on. Ottawa also paid the Saskatchewan government about $18,300,000 under hospital insurance during the last fiscal year. All provincial governments received federal financial contributions on a similar scale. This was made clear by the official opposition financial critic, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, in his brief reply to the budget last Thursday. He gave figures to show that under the former government the provinces received $3,525 million more than
[Mr. Pascoe.l

would have been paid under the Liberal government's schedule. If these payments had not been made there would have been a federal surplus in the last five years.
These remarks are by way of commenting on provincial financial responsibility. As I said earlier, they are made to emphasize my question concerning possible provincial participation in this municipal loan plan. It may be of some interest to refer to some of the comments made by the mayor of a Saskatchewan city. These comments were made before the announcement of the $10 million surplus by the Saskatchewan government. At that time he said that the Saskatchewan municipalities were in urgent need of some financial assistance from the provincial government to ease the increasing burden of municipal taxation. He hoped that the Saskatchewan government would share the increased revenue from tax rentals from Ottawa. As I say, these remarks were made before the announcement of the $10 million surplus. At that time, he said the Saskatchewan provincial government might be able to claim a reduced provincial debt, but that the debt reduction was due to a shift in the tax load from the province to the muncipal government.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I am making these comments in order to ascertain if there is some way by which the provincial governments can be brought into this plan. The Minister of Finance referred to the sewage projects which were introduced by the former government and which were a great success. He gave the figures in respect of this program. I hope he meant it, and I imagine he did, when he said that this loan program would fit in with the sewage program and would also fit in with the winter works program. Hon. members have pointed out that $900 million was paid under that winter works program, and I mention it in contrast to the $400 million available under this program.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, these comments have been cut short because the Minister of Finance explained some of the points I had in mind. However, these remarks result from inquiries I have received following the introduction of this resolution. I trust that these further questions will be cleared up by the Minister of Finance either now or when the bill is before us.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Gordon thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-76, to promote increased employment in Canada by financial assistance by way of loans to municipalities to enable municipalities to augment or accelerate municipal capital works programs.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Atlantic Development Board Act to increase the number of members of the Atlantic development board from five to eleven; to establish as a separate account in the consolidated revenue fund an Atlantic development fund to which shall be credited the sum of one hundred million dollars to be used for the purpose of financing or assisting in financing programs or projects that would contribute to the growth and development of the economy of the Atlantic region and for which satisfactory financing arrangements are not otherwise available;-

speechtext:
Well, so long as the hon. member for Lapointe will not ask me a hundred questions about it, I will try to get on with the subject very rapidly.
When the board was set up on January 24, which was over a month after the act passed, it was to set to work immediately. There has been a great deal of questioning in a good many minds as to what the relationship of the board, as it now exists, would be to the board as it is proposed to be enlarged and, in our opinion, strengthened. I think perhaps the best and simplest way I can explain that is to read a letter which I handed, after showing it to him, to the chairman of the board on May 23, 1963.
I told the chairman at the time I gave this letter to him that I intended to read it in parliament because I thought it would provide a very succinct explanation of the idea of the present administration as to how the existing board should function in the meantime, and how it would dovetail with the new arrangements that we were proposing to parliament, if those arrangements were accepted by parliament.
I was very anxious, as hon. members will see when I read the letter, to make sure any of the work the board had already embarked upon would not be interrupted pending the passage of the amending legislation. The letter reads:
May 23, 1963.
Brigadier Michael Wardell,
Chairman,
Atlantic Development Board,
Ottawa.
Dear Brigadier Wardell:
About a week ago, I told you I would advise you of the proposed amendments to the Atlantic Development Board Act as soon as my colleagues and I had reached a decision as to the form in which we proposed to recommend them to parliament.
This stage has now been reached and the appropriate resolution has already been placed on the order paper of the House of Commons.
There are two proposed amendments of a substantial character. One of these would establish an Atlantic development fund of one hundred million dollars. The board will have the responsibility of recommending the expenditure of this fund and of supervising such expenditures, but the final approval of each capital project rests with the government. The effective use of the fund will clearly require a close harmony of view between the government and the board and especially the chairman.

The other important amendment affects the membership of the board and the tenure of the members. There would be a normal tenure of three years with a provision for one renewal for a second term and with provision for staggering the initial appointments.-
Something that is quite normal in legislation of this kind.
-The four existing members of the board, apart from the chairman, would be continued in their membership by the amendment itself for one year and the present chairman would be continued for a period of two years as a member of the board. The chairman would, on the coming into force of the amending legislation, be appointed during pleasure from among the members of the board.
I would like particularly to stress the last paragraph:
Until the new legislation comes into effect it would be the hope of the government that the present board would continue to pursue any activities already undertaken and to initiate any new activities consistent with the spirit of the legislation exactly as they would have done had there been no change of government.
I may say, sir, that in proposing these amendments the government takes the view, which the previous government took in introducing the original legislation, that the board's main function is to stimulate the development of the Atlantic provinces through all kinds of existing agencies, federal, provincial, municipal, private and corporate in the Atlantic area. We believe that this is the more important of its two functions, but we indicated when we were in opposition, and we take the view now that we are in office, that the board should have at its disposal a fund which can be used to supplement its other activities.
The fund is not intended to be the sole means-even the sole means in a federal sense-of promoting development in the Atlantic provinces. I go on and say it is not intended to be the main means because it is my view that the activities of the Department of Transport, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Agriculture, the department of mines and, above all, of the new department of industry, will contribute mightily to that development.
What the Atlantic development board will do with its fund is to fill in the gaps, 1 hope; that is, do those things that none of these agencies has the specific function of doing and at the same time promote the development and emphasize the development which each of these agencies can make to the goal which I am sure all parties in the house share. I refer to the goal of bringing the level of income, the level of employment, the level of activity and the standard of living in the Atlantic provinces as rapidly as we can and as near as we can to the level in other

parts of the country. That is the objective, and I do not believe there is any quarrel with that objective-I am sure there is not -in any quarter of the house. I should be very surprised if there is.
I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that when we were in opposition we were critical of what we thought were some deficiencies in the legislation brought forward by the previous government. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton will recall that on the day the membership of the board was announced in this house by him I rose at once and welcomed the prompt appointment of the board at that time, in January. I said we hoped they would get to work quickly and we wanted to do everything we could to see that their work was fruitful and effective. I hope that in introducing amendments which we believe will strengthen the board and will give the board an opportunity to take a direct initiative to do certain things that no other agency of the federal government is equipped to do as a part of its normal operations, we will have the same spirit of co-operation from the other side of the house that we tried to manifest once the legislation had been adopted and brought into force in January of this year.
There are a great many more things that I would like to say on the bill itself. However, I would prefer, if it were possible, to have the resolution adopted and to have hon. members see the provisions of the bill itself, so we may carry on the debate in the full knowledge of what it is the government is proposing to the house. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I do not intend this evening to make any more extended observations.

I should really have mentioned that point in my explanation, Mr. Chairman. Hon. members will recall, I am sure, that the first forecast of this particular kind of measure was made in the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects in 1957, a royal commission of which the chairman was my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance. It was recommended- and I believe I have the report among my documents here and perhaps at a later stage when I speak on the bill I will put the actual recommendation on the record-that a massive effort of capital investment be made with a view, not simply to adding a little each year to the capital structure but really to add rapidly to the capital structure in the Atlantic provinces with a view to raising the level of income. This was not with the idea of having a new, permanent agency of government, but really to take a big leap forward quickly. It is that concept that we are seeking to embody in this amendment. It is for that reason it was thought that a six year period would be an appropriate one.
I think I might just add this about it. It does seem to me that if there is a short period there will be an added incentive to do as much as possible in that period. If we find that really effective results are being obtained and that this technique has not completed the work at the end of six years, I feel quite sure that whatever government may be in office in this country at that time -and none of us can tell for sure what that government will be-they will not want to stop that advance. On the other hand, if this device does not work, there is no use having another piece of governmental machinery lying around. It is for that reason that after very careful consideration this six year period was picked.

I have mentioned various departments, and I probably did not mention all that I should have, because there are other projects and my hon. friend the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, through the national parks and in other ways will, I hope, be contributing very materially to that capital investment in the Atlantic provinces, and it will not come out of this $100 million. Indeed, I have a lot of schemes for spending his money myself. I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries who has just returned from Newfoundland, where he has been to see the main fishing province of Canada, also has plans to contribute to the capital development of the Atlantic area.
I am hoping that as soon as the site of the world's fair is settled, my hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works will have an opportunity to make a tour of the coast of Newfoundland with me, especially the northeast coast, so that I can show him all the marine improvements which are necessary in order to accomplish something. I also have some plans for my hon. friend the Minister of Transport, but perhaps I have gone far enough to indicate to the hon. member for Royal that the $100 million is, in my view, a gap filler.

speechtext: I enjoyed the remarks of the minister but he has not fully clarified the situation in my mind. He mentions the sum of $100 million. Is this to be for one year, for two years, for a longer period, or for every year? All these other departments carry on with their work and we are looking forward to great decisions by them. Parks have been mentioned. Is the hon. gentleman including any of these works which would be carried on by the different departments as part of their duties? Surely we are to have $100 million over and above such sums. Will it be for the next six months, the next year, or two years, or six years?

[Mr. Pickersgill.l
months, is over and above the normal appropriation and it is intended to do things which in their normal course of operation the departments of the federal government would not be doing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breion North and Victoria):
maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO PUT QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Does the minister feel that this $100 million will give us this great leap forward of which he spoke? When will this leap forward begin, and how long will it carry on? Will it be over at the end of six years, say?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO PUT QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I think the short answer is that $100 million is $100 million more than nothing. But to answer the question a little more fully, this $100 million is not intended in any way to be substituted for any other program. It is to be an addition to what would otherwise be done.

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO PUT QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I wish to ask the minister one question. I was entranced by his kindly approach to the subject. He suggested in the last parliament that the Minister of National Revenue of that day was seducing the house in bringing forward a bill. I want to say the hon. gentleman is certainly proving to be a tremendous seducer himself. The minister has explained about the work of the different departments over and above the $100 million. What I should like to know is whether all these different departments are themselves going to inject a large extra amount of revenue into the Atlantic area as well. If not, all we end up with is $100 million, plus what we are getting today.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO PUT QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I think the present government has given a good indication of what it intends to do in other ways. The hon. member was in the house the other day when we voted a slice of the new vote for the trans-Canada highway. The present government has already indicated that in the four Atlantic provinces it intends to pay 90 per cent of the cost of completing the trans-Canada highway. I think that is good evidence of the attitude of the present government toward capital development in the Atlantic provinces. I migh say that 90 per cent of this expenditure will in itself be a sizeable sum even in comparison with the $100 million for the Atlantic development fund. As the hon. member for Cumberland knows, as the hon. member for Pictou knows, and as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough certainly knows, in their constituencies the trans-Canada highway could stand a great deal of improvement, and the sooner the better.

speechtext:
I do not propose any real changes from what was suggested on Friday. I indicated that the resolution respecting the Atlantic development board would be the second item of business for today, and we have got on to it, and I am grateful to hon. members for having let us make a start on this measure. We shall continue with it tomorrow and, I hope, get first reading of the bill, because I think it would be helpful to have the bill for study between now and the time when it could be taken up again after the budget debate.
I indicated on Friday that there would be two possibilities after that. One was the department of industry bill and the other the resolution preceding the measure respecting the Department of Agriculture. I think it will probably be more satisfactory to take the second reading of the department of industry bill, because we would probably want to start a fresh day on the Department of Agriculture measure, if we could. The department of industry has already been debated a great deal. However, should we get second reading and the committee stage of the department of industry through, then we would, perforce, start on the resolution respecting the Department of Agriculture. I hold out that bait to hon. gentlemen opposite. On Wednesday we shall begin the budget debate and carry on until it is completed.
It being two minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
